note: Published scores of other LLMs, copied from each benchmark's paper; we did not run these models. Setups differ from ours as noted, so comparisons are indicative.

benchmarks.name: Arena
benchmarks.metric: Agreement with the human vote, ties removed (guessing = 50%)
benchmarks.intro: People chat with two anonymous AI models at once and vote for the better answer. The task is to predict each person’s vote. As in the published study, ties are left out, so guessing scores 50%.
benchmarks.takeaway: Jev scores 60.5–65.1%, a few points below the published AI judges (65.0–67.7%); only the top of its range reaches Gemini 1.5 Flash. The published scores keep each model’s better result from two prompts, while Jev used one fixed prompt, and Jev’s occasional “tie” answers count as wrong.

jev_comparable.detail: same rule (ties removed); certified 98.75% interval from the 5,442 decided votes Jev answered in a uniformly random order (point estimate 62.5%); 66.0% if Jev's tie answers are left out

benchmarks.note: Published: the Arena team's PPE study, 16,038 Chatbot Arena votes from 2024; each model's better of two judge prompts. Jev: same rule on our Arena pool. Jev's certified 4-choice score (with ties and both-bad) is not comparable.

source.title: How to Evaluate Reward Models for RLHF (Frick et al., 2024)

benchmarks.name: MMLU-ProX
benchmarks.intro: Hard, university-level multiple-choice questions with up to 10 options, in 29 languages (11,759 questions per language). The score is the share answered correctly across all languages.
benchmarks.takeaway: Jev’s 73.6–77.6% overlaps the two best published models, DeepSeek-R1 (75.5%) and Qwen3-235B with thinking (74.9%), and is above GPT-4.1 (72.7%) and every other model shown. The published models were given 5 worked examples and reasoned step by step; Jev answered directly, without examples.
benchmarks.note: Same 11,759 test questions per language. Published models used 5 worked examples and step-by-step reasoning; Jev answered directly, with no examples.

benchmarks.name: HaluEval
benchmarks.metric: Accuracy, average of QA, dialogue and summarization
benchmarks.intro: Each case pairs a source text (background knowledge, a dialogue or a document) with an answer, reply or summary, and about half of these contain made-up facts. The task is to say whether it does. The score is the share judged correctly, averaged over the three tasks.
benchmarks.takeaway: Jev’s 73.4–77.4% is about 9 to 13 points above the best published result (ChatGPT, 64.5%) and above every other model shown. These results are from 2023 and older models, and their QA test did not show the evidence text that Jev was given, so part of the gap comes from the setup.
benchmarks.note: Original 2023 paper, same yes/no task on a randomly chosen correct or made-up answer; averages computed from its per-task table. Its QA prompt gave no evidence text (Jev was given it) and included examples.

benchmarks.name: AgentProcessBench
benchmarks.metric: Step accuracy over all labelled steps
benchmarks.intro: Records of AI agents working through tasks with tools, where people labelled every step the agent took as helpful, neutral or harmful. The task is to judge each step. The score is the share of steps judged correctly.
benchmarks.takeaway: Jev’s 68.9–72.8% is in the middle of the pack: level with GPT-5.2, DeepSeek-V3.2 and Kimi K2.5 (70.1–72.8%), below the top four models (74.8–81.6%) and above Qwen3-30B (68.5%) and Llama 3.3 70B (54.4%). Published models labelled a whole agent run in one call, whereas Jev judged one step at a time, and our pool leaves out the longest 31% of steps.
benchmarks.note: Published models labelled a whole trajectory in one call; Jev judged one step per call. Our pool leaves out the 31% longest steps.
